case_info.scenario: A 59-year-old male patient presented with many months of progressively worsening left nasal obstruction. He also endorsed associated occasional left occipital pain, as well as substantial unintentional weight loss. He denied any epistaxis and had no significant history of alcohol or tobacco use. Physical examination revealed a papillomatous-appearing mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the maxillofacial region demonstrated a large, heterogeneously enhancing lesion occupying the left nasal cavity, left orbit, and bilateral pterygopalatine fossae (Figure 1A). The mass crossed the midline into the right nasal cavity and nasopharynx, with thin and subtle left frontal dural enhancement, suggesting early intracranial extension. A biopsy of the left nasal cavity lesion was performed in the clinic. Gross examination of the incisional specimen revealed irregular, polypoid fragments of soft tissue, measuring up to 1.5 cm in greatest dimension. Histologic examination demonstrated an epithelial proliferation with squamous differentiation and papillary and blunt bulbous architecture (Figure 1B). Cytologic atypia and increased mitotic figures were observed (Figure 1C). Conventional invasion was not identified in the biopsy material, nor was lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Ancillary testing was performed, and the tumor cell results were negative for p16, CD99, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) RNA in situ hybridization. They demonstrated focal positivity for low-risk HPV RNA in situ hybridization.

B, Incisional biopsy demonstrated a malignant squamous epithelial proliferation with bulky papillary and endophytic architecture (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification, ×4). C, Image demonstrates cytologic atypia and several mitotic figures (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification, ×20).
case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 59-year-old male patient presented with many months of progressively worsening left nasal obstruction. He also endorsed associated occasional left occipital pain, as well as substantial unintentional weight loss. He denied any epistaxis and had no significant history of alcohol or tobacco use. Physical examination revealed a papillomatous-appearing mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the maxillofacial region demonstrated a large, heterogeneously enhancing lesion occupying the left nasal cavity, left orbit, and bilateral pterygopalatine fossae (Figure 1A). The mass crossed the midline into the right nasal cavity and nasopharynx, with thin and subtle left frontal dural enhancement, suggesting early intracranial extension. A biopsy of the left nasal cavity lesion was performed in the clinic. Gross examination of the incisional specimen revealed irregular, polypoid fragments of soft tissue, measuring up to 1.5 cm in greatest dimension. Histologic examination demonstrated an epithelial proliferation with squamous differentiation and papillary and blunt bulbous architecture (Figure 1B). Cytologic atypia and increased mitotic figures were observed (Figure 1C). Conventional invasion was not identified in the biopsy material, nor was lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Ancillary testing was performed, and the tumor cell results were negative for p16, CD99, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) RNA in situ hybridization. They demonstrated focal positivity for low-risk HPV RNA in situ hybridization.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Based on the clinical presentation and histopathologic findings, I believe the most appropriate next step in management is to consider this lesion as a papillary squamous cell carcinoma (option A). The malignant features, including cytologic atypia, increased mitotic figures, and the overall architectural patterns observed in the biopsy suggest a malignant process, despite the absence of conventional invasion. The significant weight loss and progressive nasal obstruction reinforce the likelihood of malignancy. Further staging and treatment planning, including surgical intervention or oncological referral, should follow.

I agree that malignancy is highly probable given the clinical and histologic features. However, papillary squamous cell carcinoma is typically positive for high-risk HPV, whereas this tumor is negative for p16 and high-risk HPV, showing only focal low-risk HPV positivity. This discrepancy suggests we should consider other sinonasal malignancies with papillary architecture, such as sinonasal papilloma with dysplasia/carcinoma ex papilloma or a non-HPV-related squamous cell carcinoma variant.

You make a compelling argument regarding the HPV status, which indeed warrants reconsideration of the diagnosis. Given the lack of high-risk HPV positivity and the architectural features, a diagnosis of squamous papilloma (option B) with possible dysplastic changes may be more fitting. I will reflect on staging implications and management for this diagnosis moving forward.

While squamous papilloma is a consideration, the presence of significant cytologic atypia and increased mitoses, especially in the context of weight loss and intracranial extension on imaging, pushes the diagnosis beyond a simple benign papilloma. A sinonasal papilloma with high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma ex papilloma is more likely, which still carries malignant potential and requires complete surgical resection with clear margins.

You raise valid points regarding the implications of the significant cytologic atypia and increased mitotic figures, suggesting that we may indeed be dealing with a sinonasal papilloma exhibiting high-grade dysplasia or even a malignant variant. I appreciate the emphasis on the need for complete surgical resection due to the potential malignancy, but I still lean towards the diagnosis of squamous papilloma with dysplasia at this stage, given the histologic features and HPV findings. We should discuss the surgical intervention plan further.

That's a reasonable interim assessment, and complete surgical resection is indeed the critical next step, regardless of the precise label, to obtain a full histologic evaluation. The definitive diagnosis—whether high-grade dysplastic papilloma or carcinoma ex papilloma—will rely on examination of the entire resected specimen to assess for invasion, which the biopsy may have missed.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 9.3. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 59-year-old male patient presented with many months of progressively worsening left nasal obstruction. He also endorsed associated occasional left occipital pain, as well as substantial unintentional weight loss. He denied any epistaxis and had no significant history of alcohol or tobacco use. Physical examination revealed a papillomatous-appearing mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the maxillofacial region demonstrated a large, heterogeneously enhancing lesion occupying the left nasal cavity, left orbit, and bilateral pterygopalatine fossae (Figure 1A). The mass crossed the midline into the right nasal cavity and nasopharynx, with thin and subtle left frontal dural enhancement, suggesting early intracranial extension. A biopsy of the left nasal cavity lesion was performed in the clinic. Gross examination of the incisional specimen revealed irregular, polypoid fragments of soft tissue, measuring up to 1.5 cm in greatest dimension. Histologic examination demonstrated an epithelial proliferation with squamous differentiation and papillary and blunt bulbous architecture (Figure 1B). Cytologic atypia and increased mitotic figures were observed (Figure 1C). Conventional invasion was not identified in the biopsy material, nor was lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Ancillary testing was performed, and the tumor cell results were negative for p16, CD99, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) RNA in situ hybridization. They demonstrated focal positivity for low-risk HPV RNA in situ hybridization.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

Based on the clinical presentation and histopathologic findings, I believe the most appropriate next step in management is to consider this lesion as a papillary squamous cell carcinoma (option A). The significant weight loss and progressive nasal obstruction reinforce the likelihood of malignancy. Further staging and treatment planning, including surgical intervention or oncological referral, should follow.

I agree that malignancy is highly probable given the clinical and histologic features. However, papillary squamous cell carcinoma is typically positive for high-risk HPV, whereas this tumor is negative for p16 and high-risk HPV, showing only focal low-risk HPV positivity. This discrepancy suggests we should consider other sinonasal malignancies with papillary architecture, such as sinonasal papilloma with dysplasia/carcinoma ex papilloma or a non-HPV-related squamous cell carcinoma variant.

You make a compelling argument regarding the HPV status, which indeed warrants reconsideration of the diagnosis. Given the lack of high-risk HPV positivity and the architectural features, a diagnosis of squamous papilloma (option B) with possible dysplastic changes may be more fitting. I will reflect on staging implications and management for this diagnosis moving forward.

While squamous papilloma is a consideration, the presence of significant cytologic atypia and increased mitoses, especially in the context of weight loss and intracranial extension on imaging, pushes the diagnosis beyond a simple benign papilloma. A sinonasal papilloma with high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma ex papilloma is more likely, which still carries malignant potential and requires complete surgical resection with clear margins.

I appreciate the emphasis on the need for complete surgical resection due to the potential malignancy, but I still lean towards the diagnosis of squamous papilloma with dysplasia at this stage, given the histologic features and HPV findings. We should discuss the surgical intervention plan further.

That's a reasonable interim assessment, and complete surgical resection is indeed the critical next step, regardless of the precise label, to obtain a full histologic evaluation. The definitive diagnosis—whether high-grade dysplastic papilloma or carcinoma ex papilloma—will rely on examination of the entire resected specimen to assess for invasion, which the biopsy may have missed.

However, I still find the diagnosis of squamous papilloma with possible dysplasia more fitting at this stage, especially considering the histologic findings and HPV results. Surgical intervention remains critical, and we can reassess the diagnosis based on the full resected specimen findings post-operatively. Let's plan for that intervention promptly.

Agreed. Planning for prompt, complete surgical resection is the definitive management step, as it will provide the final diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. The key will be to evaluate the entire lesion for definitive invasion, which will clarify if this is a high-grade dysplastic papilloma or an invasive carcinoma, guiding any adjuvant therapy.

Let's proceed with planning for surgical intervention as priority.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10
